result: I concluded that the CH₂Cl₂ solvent is disordered and the rest of the structure is ordered, so I submitted a two-orientation model for the solvent. In the original model its Cl atoms had very large, elongated displacement parameters (Ueq 0.19–0.24 Å², anisotropy up to 3.3), and there were symmetric residual peaks about 0.7 Å on either side of each Cl. That is the usual sign of a smeared solvent site. I modelled it as two CH₂Cl₂ orientations, Cl2/Cl3/C43 in PART 1 and Cl2B/Cl3B/C43B in PART 2. Their occupancies are tied to one free variable and refined to 0.71/0.29. Each part has riding H atoms and SADI/DFIX, SIMU, RIGU and ISOR restraints. This lowered R1 from 0.0534 to 0.0512 and wR2 from 0.142 to 0.135 with 28 extra parameters, which a rough Hamilton R-factor ratio test suggests is significant. The improvement is modest, though, and the model is not clean. The two orientations lie only about 0.4–0.9 Å apart, the Cl Ueq values are still high (~0.17 Å²), and the largest residual peak (1.15 e/Å³, about 1.9 Å from Cl3) is still unexplained. Models that placed solvent atoms on that peak gave chemically impossible geometry or ADPs that blew up, so I dropped them. The ~0.9 e/Å³ peaks 1.1 Å from the Fe on the special position look like heavy-atom ripple, and the elongated outer naphthyl carbons (C5–C7) have no matching difference density. I left both of those unchanged.
